language_wrapper: A generalized SET deck is built as follows: there are {d} independent attributes, and each attribute can take one of {q} distinct values. Every possible attribute-value profile appears exactly once, so the deck has {q}^{d} cards. A q-card selection is called complementary if, for each attribute, across the chosen q cards either all values are identical or all {q} values appear exactly once. How many complementary q-card sets are there that have exactly {t} attributes varying (i.e., using all {q} values) and the remaining {d_minus_t} attributes constant across the set?
hardness_rationale: The seed counts all complementary triples in the 3x3x3 SET deck, which reduces to counting affine lines in F_3^3. The augmented family requires counting complementary q-card sets in F_q^d with the additional constraint that exactly t attributes vary (are bijective along the set). Solving demands recognizing the affine-line model over F_q, classifying lines by the support of their direction vectors, counting one-dimensional subspaces with a specified Hamming weight, and then accounting for parallel translations. This is a more advanced combinatorial and linear-algebraic decomposition than the seed’s undifferentiated line count, and resists ad hoc guessing due to the parameter t.
notes: Proof sketch: Model each card as a vector in F_q^d by encoding the value of each attribute j as an element of F_q. A q-card set is complementary if and only if it is an affine line L = {a + sv : s in F_q} with some base point a in F_q^d and a nonzero direction v in F_q^d, because for each coordinate j, the sequence a_j + s v_j is either constant (v_j = 0) or a bijection onto F_q (v_j ≠ 0). Thus, a complementary set corresponds exactly to an affine one-dimensional subspace (a line) of F_q^d. The number of such lines, without restriction, is q^{d-1} * (q^d - 1)/(q - 1): choose a direction up to scaling (there are (q^d - 1)/(q - 1) one-dimensional subspaces through the origin), and for each direction choose a translate (there are q^{d} / q = q^{d-1} distinct cosets). Now impose the constraint that exactly t attributes vary across the set. This means exactly t coordinates of v are nonzero (equivalently, the support of v has size t). The number of nonzero vectors with support exactly t is C(d, t) * (q - 1)^t. Modding out by nonzero scalars identifies each one-dimensional subspace with an orbit of size q - 1 under scaling, so the number of distinct directions with weight t is C(d, t) * (q - 1)^{t - 1}. For each such direction, there are q^{d-1} parallel lines (cosets). Therefore the total number of complementary q-sets with exactly t varying attributes is q^{d-1} * C(d, t) * (q - 1)^{t - 1}. Summing over t = 1..d recovers the classical count q^{d-1} * (q^d - 1)/(q - 1). This generalizes the seed (q = d = 3) and recovers 117 upon summation, while the t-refined counts are new and require the direction-weight classification.
source_question: Every card in a deck has a picture of one shape - circle, square, or triangle, which is painted in one of the three colors - red, blue, or green. Furthermore, each color is applied in one of three shades - light, medium, or dark. The deck has 27 cards, with every shape-color-shade combination represented. A set of three cards from the deck is called complementary if all of the following statements are true: i. Either each of the three cards has a different shape or all three of the card have the same shape. ii. Either each of the three cards has a different color or all three of the cards have the same color. iii. Either each of the three cards has a different shade or all three of the cards have the same shade. How many different complementary three-card sets are there?
